title: Centre of Mass
short_intro: The centre of mass is a unique point in a system of particles or an extended body where the entire mass is considered to be concentrated for describing translational motion. It behaves as if all external forces are applied directly at this point.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of centre of mass for discrete particle systems, symmetric rigid bodies, motion of centre of mass, conservation of linear momentum, and internal forces.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Continuous mass distributions, use of integration for irregular objects, variable mass systems, frame of reference transformations, and centre of mass in central force problems.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Position Vector
bullets: For a discrete system of particles, the position vector R of the centre of mass is given by the weighted average of the position vectors of the individual particles.
R = (sum(m_i r_i)) / (sum(m_i)), where m_i is the mass of the i-th particle and r_i is its position vector.
The centre of mass depends solely on the mass distribution and is independent of the coordinate system chosen.

concept_notes.heading: Motion of the Centre of Mass
bullets: The total external force acting on a system equals the total mass of the system multiplied by the acceleration of its centre of mass: F_ext = M A_cm.
Internal forces between particles cancel out in pairs due to Newton's third law and do not affect the acceleration of the centre of mass.
If the net external force is zero, the centre of mass moves with a constant velocity, or remains at rest, regardless of internal motion.

concept_notes.heading: Centre of Mass for Continuous Bodies
bullets: For continuous mass distributions, summation is replaced by integration: R = (1 / M) int r dm.
In Cartesian coordinates, the coordinates are X_cm = (1 / M) int x dm, Y_cm = (1 / M) int y dm, and Z_cm = (1 / M) int z dm.
Symmetric objects with uniform density have their centre of mass located at their geometric center.

concept_notes.heading: Centre of Mass Frame (C-Frame)
bullets: A reference frame attached to the centre of mass is known as the centre of mass frame or zero-momentum frame.
In this frame, the total linear momentum of the system is always zero.
It significantly simplifies the analysis of collisions, two-body central force problems, and rotational dynamics.

derivations.title: Position Vector of Centre of Mass for a Two-Particle System
derivations.conditions: Two point masses m_1 and m_2 located at position vectors r_1 and r_2.
steps: Define the total mass of the system as M = m_1 + m_2.
Apply the definition of the centre of mass position vector for discrete masses: R = (m_1 r_1 + m_2 r_2) / (m_1 + m_2).
Differentiate the position vector with respect to time to obtain the velocity of the centre of mass: V_cm = (m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2) / M.
Differentiate again with respect to time to get the acceleration of the centre of mass: A_cm = (m_1 a_1 + m_2 a_2) / M.

derivations.title: Centre of Mass of a Uniform Semicircular Ring
derivations.conditions: Uniform semicircular ring of radius R and total mass M lying in the xy-plane.
steps: Consider a differential mass element dm corresponding to an angular element d\theta at angle \theta, where dm = (M / \pi) d\theta.
The coordinates of the mass element are x = R \cos\theta and y = R \sin\theta.
By symmetry about the y-axis, the x-coordinate of the centre of mass, X_cm = 0.
Evaluate the y-coordinate using integration: Y_cm = (1 / M) int y dm = (1 / M) int_0^\pi (R \sin\theta) (M / \pi) d\theta.
Simplify the integral: Y_cm = (R / \pi) int_0^\pi \sin\theta d\theta = (R / \pi) [-\cos\theta]_0^\pi = 2R / \pi.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Explosion of a Projectile in Mid-Air
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic trajectory of a projectile with a dotted continuation representing the unexploded path, and fragment trajectories diverging symmetrically around the continuing parabolic path of the centre of mass.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Internal forces causing an explosion do not affect the trajectory of the centre of mass, which continues to follow the original parabola under gravity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in TGT and numerically in PGT regarding fragment landing positions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Two-Body System on a Smooth Surface
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two blocks of unequal masses connected by a spring on a frictionless horizontal floor, showing displacement vectors from a fixed origin to the individual masses and their common centre of mass.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that in the absence of external horizontal forces, the centre of mass remains stationary while internal oscillations occur.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to evaluate understanding of internal vs external forces and conservation of momentum.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Suspension Method for Finding Centre of Gravity
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An irregular lamina suspended from a pinhole with a plumb line hanging vertically downwards, intersecting the lamina along a straight line.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The centre of gravity (and hence centre of mass in a uniform gravitational field) always lies on the vertical line passing through the point of suspension.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Laboratory-based conceptual question in TGT exams.

solved_numericals.question: Three point masses of 1 kg, 2 kg, and 3 kg are located at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1 m. Find the coordinates of the centre of mass, placing the 1 kg mass at the origin.
solution_steps: Set coordinate system: 1 kg at (0, 0), 2 kg at (1, 0), and 3 kg at (0.5, \sqrt{3}/2).
Calculate X_cm = (m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2 + m_3 x_3) / (m_1 + m_2 + m_3).
Calculate Y_cm = (m_1 y_1 + m_2 y_2 + m_3 y_3) / (1 + 2 + 3).

solved_numericals.question: A uniform circular disc of radius R has a circular hole of radius R/2 cut from it. The centre of the hole is at a distance R/2 from the centre of the original disc. Find the position of the centre of mass of the remaining portion.
solution_steps: Let the mass of the complete disc be M and surface mass density be \sigma.
The area of the complete disc is A_1 = \pi R^2, so M_1 = M.
The radius of the removed circular hole is R/2, so its area is A_2 = \pi (R/2)^2 = \pi R^2 / 4 = A_1 / 4.
The mass of the removed portion is M_2 = M / 4.
Let the centre of the original disc be at the origin (0, 0). Place the centre of the hole at (R/2, 0).
Use the formula for the centre of mass of the remaining part: X_cm = (M_1 X_1 - M_2 X_2) / (M_1 - M_2).
solved_numericals.answer: -R/6 from the centre of the original disc along the line joining the centres

solved_numericals.question: A man of mass 60 kg is standing at one end of a 2 m long boat of mass 140 kg floating in still water. If the man walks to the other end of the boat, through what distance does the boat move relative to the water?
solution_steps: Total mass M = m_man + m_boat = 60 + 140 = 200 kg.
Since no external horizontal force acts on the system (man + boat), the centre of mass remains at rest.
Let the displacement of the boat relative to the water be x. The displacement of the man relative to the water is (L - x), where L = 2 m.
Apply the condition for zero displacement of the centre of mass: m_man (L - x) - m_boat x = 0.

assumptions_and_limitations: The centre of mass concept assumes macroscopic bodies where classical mechanics is valid, ignoring quantum mechanical wave-packet spreading.
In extended bodies, the gravitational centre of mass (centre of gravity) coincides with the geometric centre of mass only if the gravitational field is uniform across the entire body.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The centre of mass of a body must always lie inside the material of the body.
common_misconceptions.correct: The centre of mass can lie outside the physical body, as seen in hollow objects like rings, hollow spheres, and L-shaped brackets.
common_misconceptions.why: The definition R = (1/M) int r dm relies on mass distribution in space, not on material continuity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Internal forces can change the velocity of the centre of mass of a system.
common_misconceptions.correct: Internal forces can only change the relative positions and velocities of individual particles within the system, leaving the centre of mass motion unaffected.
common_misconceptions.why: According to Newton's third law, internal forces occur in equal and opposite pairs that cancel out when summing forces for the entire system.

quick_revision: The centre of mass is the point where the entire mass of a system is assumed to be concentrated for translational motion analysis.
Centre of Mass (Discrete): R_{cm} = \frac{\sum m_i r_i}{\sum m_i}
Centre of Mass (Continuous): R_{cm} = \frac{1}{M} \int r \, dm
